facts.fact: A bacterial bloom is the most likely cause of milky water and is common in new tanks.
A mature bacterial ecosystem in an aquarium takes much longer than six months to develop.
A bacterial bloom in a new tank is generally not dangerous. Biological filtration can take four to six weeks to mature.
Green water is caused by free-floating single-celled algae multiplying fast. The bloom can lower dissolved oxygen and affect fish health.
Vietnamese keepers call white bacterial cloudiness 'vi sinh nở hoa' or 'bùng vi sinh'.
In a bacterial bloom the water suddenly turns cloudy, like rice-washing water ('nước vo gạo').
Many keepers mistake a bacterial bloom for their beneficial bacteria dying off ('chết vi sinh').
White or grey cloudiness from unwashed gravel or stirred-up substrate in a new setup usually clears within 1–2 days with filtration.
Green or discoloured water can appear even when test readings look normal.
Causes of cloudy water include microscopic debris the filter cannot catch, minerals leaching from décor and substrate in acidic water, and bacterial blooms.
Overfeeding, an unnoticed dead fish, infrequent water changes and swings in water chemistry can trigger a bloom.
Over-cleaning the filter can kill beneficial bacteria and let bloom bacteria take over.
Over-cleaning or replacing filter media often removes beneficial bacteria and can cause white cloudiness.
Antiseptic or antibiotic treatments can kill beneficial bacteria or break the nitrogen cycle, causing a bacterial bloom, especially in new tanks.
Sudden water changes, tank cleaning, medicines, sudden changes in temperature or pH, and adding more fish can trigger a bacterial bloom.
Green water can be caused by direct sunlight, lights on for more than 8–12 hours a day, non-aquarium lights, or planted-tank lights on a tank without plants.
Too many fish or infrequent cleaning raises phosphate and nitrate levels, which feed algae.
Excess nutrients or fish waste that overwhelm the biological filter, high phosphate, a cycling tank, and overstocking can all lead to green or cloudy water.
Strong light, especially direct sun on tanks near windows or outdoors, combined with excess nutrients drives green water.
Test ammonia first; it should read zero. Check the water temperature too.
If the cloudiness is only a bacterial bloom and ammonia is zero, do nothing and let the tank rebalance.
Stop feeding for about 7 days. Healthy fish should cope.
Leave the filter alone, with no cleaning or other changes, for at least 7 days.
Ammonia or nitrite readings above zero can mean a mini-cycle is feeding the bloom. Test daily during recovery.
Add a layer of filter wool to trap debris too fine for standard media.
Seachem Clarity dose: 5 mL (one capful) per 80 L, about 20 US gallons. That works out to 2.5 mL per 40 L and 12.5 mL per 200 L.
Cloudiness may increase for a while after dosing Clarity. Seachem says this is normal and the water should clear within 1–2 hours.
After Clarity has cleared the tank, clean the filter floss or cartridge to remove the trapped material.
API Accu-Clear is a flocculant that clumps particles so they settle for siphoning or are caught by the filter. API gives no dose online; follow the label.
For algae, a UV sterilizer can help. Add fine filter floss to catch dead algae particles.
UV-C light (200–280 nm) damages the DNA of free-floating algae and bacteria so they cannot reproduce.
Recommended UV dose for algae and bacteria is 180,000 µWs/cm². Use a unit rated for the tank's volume; undersized units do not work, oversized ones are fine.
Replace the UV bulb every six months.
UV does not affect organisms attached to surfaces or living inside fish.
API suggests its algaecide AlgaeFix to clear green water quickly, and Stress Zyme or Quick Start bacteria to compete with algae for nutrients.
Combine mechanical, biological and chemical filtration (activated carbon, zeolite) and a filter with a UV lamp to fight green water.
Step 1: test the water for nitrogen cycling and high phosphate.
Step 2: do a 30% partial water change with a gravel siphon and scrape algae off the glass and décor.
Step 3: add beneficial bacteria. Step 4: if still cloudy, use a flocculant.
Next steps: add live plants to absorb nutrients. If cloudiness persists, review fish numbers and size against tank volume, and keep testing and changing water consistently.
Do weekly water changes of 10–25%.
Do regular 10–50% water changes. Never change 100% of the water.
Limit tank lighting to roughly 8–12 hours a day and move the tank out of direct sunlight.
Change about 25–30% of the water weekly, matching the new water's temperature and quality to the tank's.
Use curtains, plants or a new tank position to keep direct sun off the tank, and limit feeding.
Keep temperature and pH stable, keep a suitable number of fish, and provide enough aeration.
In a mature tank, ammonia and nitrite should read 0. Nitrate should rise slowly, and pH and KH should drop slowly.
Avoid large, irregular water changes such as 75%, which can destabilize the tank.
Common mistakes include deep-cleaning the tank and accessories, overfeeding, overstocking and adding unwashed gravel.
Over-the-counter water-based antibiotics are typically unlicensed and can harm fish.
Adding antiseptics or antibiotics to the tank kills beneficial bacteria, and setting up a tank before the nitrogen cycle is stable invites blooms.
Using chemicals wrongly during cleaning can lower dissolved oxygen and cloud the water.
A Vietnamese source lists sudden temperature changes, especially in warm water, among the triggers of bacterial blooms.
Vietnamese shops widely sell beneficial-bacteria products ('men vi sinh', e.g. Aquarium Care) to rebalance tanks after a bloom.
Tanks near windows or outdoors in direct sun are singled out as prone to green water.
Practical Fishkeeping says blooms usually clear on their own within a few days, so heavy intervention such as big water changes is not needed.
A Vietnamese seller claims heterotrophic bacteria double every 15–20 minutes, but gives no source.
